poses.title: Achilles Stretch
paragraphs: Ankle mobility is a huge problem for many people. Most of these people do not even realize that they have this problem. I know this because I was one of them. For years, I struggled with squats and I never fully understood why. My hip mobility was fine. Eventually, I discovered it was due to poor ankle mobility. This stretch will greatly improve your ability to practice dorsiflexion of the ankle joint — allowing for deeper squats and greater overall mobility.

Begin facing the tree — about 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk. There are several ways to go about this. First, you can keep both feet the same distance from the tree. Second, you can stagger the feet, with one foot slightly in front of the other. Further, you can practice this pose dynamically or statically. When practicing dynamically, exhale as you bend the knees and dorsiflex at the ankles. Inhale as you return to the starting position. When practicing statically, hold the position with the ankles in dorsiflexion while breathing deeply. You can also incorporate some gentle side-to-side movement here. A circular motion works wonders as well.

poses.title: Balancing Half Moon Pose
paragraphs: Very few people can practice the full expression of this pose. However, with the tree, it is possible for everyone. Begin an arm’s length away from the tree, then step back an additional 1 or 2 feet. Plant one foot with the toes facing towards the trunk. With the same-side arm, reach for the tree and plant the hand on the trunk. With the other hand on the hip, begin to lift the other leg. The hips, belly button, and toes of the lifted leg should be perpendicular to the toes of the planted foot. Taking the hand from the hip, extend the arm up. Reach through the fingertips and press back through the heel of the lifted leg to create maximum space. Practice for a couple of breaths on each side — mindfully entering, and mindfully exiting.

poses.title: Balancing Revolved Half Moon Pose
paragraphs: Again, this is an extremely challenging pose. I was not able to do this pose myself until I enlisted the help of the trees. This is one of the hardest balancing postures in Yoga, and very few people even attempt to practice. However, with Tree Yoga, you can easily get yourself into it, and you can prime the nervous system for greater balance and stronger stability.

Begin an arm’s length away from the tree, then step back an additional 1 or 2 feet. You want to be facing the tree, with the toes towards the trunk. Root down through one foot and place the opposite-side hand on the tree. Extend the other leg back. Keeping the core engaged and the spine long, twist open towards the planted leg. Reach up through the fingertips for maximum length. Press the other hand into the tree, and also press back through the heel of the lifted leg. Practice for a couple of breaths on each side.

poses.title: Big Toe Pose
paragraphs: This pose simultaneously improves balance and stretches the muscles of the inner thigh. It is not just a beautiful pose, but rather it actually strengthens the foundation of stability, and lengthens muscles that are chronically tight in many people. Do not forget about stretching the groin. Any tightness in the body eventually leads to problems. We want to be flexible throughout.

Begin with the side body facing the tree. You can either grab the outside of the trunk, or you can plant the hand. Root down through the foot closest to the tree, and lift the other leg. Grab on to the big toe of the lifted leg with the “ peace fingers” of the outside arm. Alternatively, you can grab on to the inside of the foot with the hand. Extend the leg up and out to the side. Use the tree to help you develop balance, and keep the spine long. Practice for several breaths on each side.

poses.title: Bioenergetic Bouncing
paragraphs: People are often holding on to energies that they do not need. The mind-body connection is a two-way street, and you can easily release negative energy by shaking out the body. Begin in a standing position, relatively close to the tree. Start to gently bounce up and down on the balls of the feet. The balls of the feet do not need to lift completely up and off the ground, but they can. It helps to pretend you are jump roping, but there is nothing to hold. Thus, you can — and should — relax the body as much as possible. Your level of relaxation determines your ability to release negative energy. Let go of all stress. Breathe deeply as you continue to bounce.

poses.title: Bridge Pose
paragraphs: Begin facing away from the tree in a supine position, with the knees bent and the feet down. The feet should be hip-width apart. A common mistake is placing the feet too far apart. The head should be about a foot away from the tree. Reach the arms back and grab the trunk. Press down through the heels and drive the hips up on an exhalation. On an inhalation, slowly lower the hips down. Practice this move dynamically — moving with the breath. Additionally, practice this move statically — holding for several breaths at the top. You can also practice this with the arms relaxed by the sides. For a greater challenge, practice this with one leg at a time.

poses.title: Calf Raises
paragraphs: Having strong legs is important. It is the foundation of the body, and the foundation of the leg is the calf and foot. The most important part of any structure is the foundation. Make sure your calves and feet are solid and strong, otherwise you will have a hard time finding stability in all poses, as well as in your reality. Further, you will be easily knocked over by the winds of life. Establish a foundation as strong as the roots of a tree, and you will be able to handle any storm or situation.

Begin facing the tree, about 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk. The toes can be directly facing the trunk, or they can be slightly angled in or out. Depending on the position of the toes, you will work different parts of the calves and feet. As for the hands, they should be connected to the tree. On an exhalation, press up onto the toes — fully contracting the calves. On an inhalation, slowly return to the starting position. Be mindful not to roll onto the outsides of the feet. Instead, drive down through the big toe mound.

poses.title: Chair Pose
paragraphs: Begin facing away from the tree, with your back against the trunk. Alternatively, you could also do this pose facing the tree, with the hands on the trunk. The feet should be about hip-width apart. For a greater challenge, you can bring the feet together. Bend the knees, and lower the hips down. Keep length in the spine, and hold this position statically for a couple rounds of breath.

Chair pose is very challenging for many people. It is difficult to get deeply into the pose, and it is hard to keep the spine long. Practicing this pose with the tree allows you to get deeper than you thought possible — priming the nervous system for better mobility and improved biomechanics. It also keeps the spine in perfect posture. This pose will also build tremendous strength in the legs.

poses.title: Chest Stretch
paragraphs: Having a strong chest is good, but having a tight chest is not. A lot of people have a tight front body and a weak back body. This results in the body collapsing in on itself. Do not allow this to happen. When the body collapses in on itself, you put yourself in fight-or-flight. Keep the front body open.

Begin an arm’s length away from the tree, with the side body facing the trunk. Plant the inside-hand on the tree, with the arm angled up 45 degrees. This angle provides the best stretch for the chest because it is the way the muscle fibers run in that area. Keep the hand planted on the tree as you gently turn away from the trunk. Maintain strong posture and take several deep breaths. Practice on both sides.

poses.title: Child’s Pose
paragraphs: Begin in tabletop position, facing the tree. The head should be only a few inches away from the trunk. Bring the knees out slightly wider than the hips, and bring the toes closer together. Next, shift the weight back and sit on top of the feet. Reach the arms in front of you and grab onto the base of the tree. Maintain a long spine. Consciously relax the body as much as possible, and take several deep breaths. Expand the breath in all directions — not just into the belly. Expand into the back body and the side bodies as well.

poses.title: Dancer’s Pose
paragraphs: It is truly amazing how much deeper you can get into this pose with the help of a tree. The opening of the hips and the stretching of the hip flexors in this posture is second to none. As with other challenging balance poses, use the tree to help you find balance, and then cultivate more of it over time.

Begin an arm ’ s length away from the tree, then step back an additional 1 or 2 feet. Root down through one foot, with the toes facing the trunk. With the same-side arm, reach for the tree and plant the hand. Use the other arm to reach for the inside of the foot on the other leg — the leg that is not planted down. Alternatively, you can grab the outside of the foot. Utilize the tree to help you balance as you kick the lifted leg back and up. You should feel a huge stretch in the hips. Breathe like this for a couple of moments, then practice on the other side. Enter and exit mindfully.

poses.title: Diagonal Lunge
paragraphs: This is one of my personal favorite lunge variations, and it is so much better with the tree. The stretch in the side body and in the hip flexors can get incredibly deep. You can create so much space in the lateral chain, and you can really feel the stretch all the way from head to toe.

Begin on the side of the tree, with the hand of the inside arm on the trunk. Keep whichever leg is closest to the tree planted down. Take the outside leg back, and diagonally across towards the tree. Bend the lead knee closest to the tree, and slowly drop the hips down. Next, keeping the spine elongated, side bend towards the tree — taking the hand of the outside arm to the trunk if possible. Stay here for a couple of breaths. Then, drive down through the lead heel on an exhalation to return to standing. Practice on the other side as well.

poses.title: Dips
paragraphs: This move requires a special type of tree. Find a tree with exposed roots or strong horizontal branches that are low to the ground. It should also be relatively level, but it doesn’t have to be perfect. With the back facing the roots or horizontal branch, place the hands down on the tree about shoulder-width apart. The fingertips should be going towards the hips. Either have the knees bent and the feet down, or have the legs fully extended with just the heels down. Shift the body forward slightly, and keep the hips lifted the entire time. On an inhalation, bend the elbows and lower the body down. On an exhalation, press back up to the starting position — using the triceps. Keep the arms tucked in close to the body, as opposed to flaring the elbows out. For a greater challenge, you can also practice this move with the gymnastics rings hanging from a strong branch.

poses.title: Downward-Facing Dog
paragraphs: Begin in tabletop position, relatively close to the trunk. You can practice this pose facing towards the tree, or facing away. Curl the toes under, and lift the knees. Pike the hips up and shift the weight back. You do not want the hands supporting most of your weight. You really want to shift the weight back towards the feet as much as possible. The arms should be straight, but not locked out. The face should be relaxed. Find some gentle movement in this position — bending one knee at a time, and melting alternate heels down to the ground. Then, settle into a static stretch — pressing both heels down at the same time. Practice for a couple of breaths.

poses.title: Dynamic Twisting
paragraphs: Begin about an arm’s length away from the tree. On an inhalation, bring the left arm forward and place the hand on the right side of the trunk. At the same time, extend the right arm behind. On an exhalation, use the hand on the trunk as leverage to twist open to the right — reaching farther behind you with the right arm. Next, on an inhalation, untwist and bring the right arm forward. Place the right hand on the left side of the trunk, and mindfully swing the left arm behind. On an exhalation, use the hand on the tree as leverage again to twist open to the left. Make this movement as fluid as possible as you alternate sides. It should feel as if you are swimming through the air. Practice for several breaths.

poses.title: Easy Pose
paragraphs: Start in a seated position, facing away from the tree. Criss-cross the legs as you bring the back against the trunk. The entire back should be as close as possible to the tree. Do not allow yourself to slouch. Instead, use the tree to help you maintain good posture. Relax the arms down by the sides, and take several deep breaths. Most people do not realize that there are actually 2 ways to criss-cross the legs. Have you ever noticed that whenever you cross the legs that the same leg is typically on top? Make sure you practice this pose with the other leg on top as well — criss-crossed the other way.

poses.title: Extended Side Angle Pose
paragraphs: Begin facing the tree with the feet very close to the trunk — a few inches or less. Keep one foot next to the tree, with the toes pointed directly at the trunk. Keep the same-side hand on the tree as well. Step back with the other leg. The back heel should be melted down to the ground, with the toes angled out. Keeping the back leg straight, bend the front knee and drop the hips. Take the arm closest to the tree and reach down towards the ground — placing the hand just inside the foot. Take the other arm over the head and grab the trunk of the tree. Use the hand on the tree as leverage to tilt the chest and shoulder up. This results in a huge opening of the side body. Stay here for a couple of breaths, then practice on the other side.

poses.title: Eyes-Closed Balance Pose
paragraphs: Balancing with the eyes open can be tough, but balancing with the eyes closed takes it to the next level. For most people, it is a challenge to balance for just a couple of seconds with the eyes closed. Use the tree to help you find balance. By doing this, you can cultivate greater balance than you ever thought possible.

Begin an arm’s length away from the tree, with the side body facing the trunk. Root down through the foot closest to the trunk as you place the same-side hand on the tree. Close the eyes, and lift the other foot. Alternatively, you can keep both feet in contact with the ground, and shift more weight towards the foot closest to the trunk instead of lifting the other foot entirely if that helps you in the beginning. To develop better balance, get progressively lighter with the hand on the trunk — to the point where you only have one finger in contact with the tree. Eventually, you can let go completely. Practice balancing for a couple of breaths on each side.

poses.title: Forearm Stand
paragraphs: Begin in tabletop position, facing away from the tree, and with the feet close to the trunk. Next, make a strong foundation with the forearms. They should be parallel, and about shoulder-width apart. It is helpful to gently press the forearms away from each other, in addition to actively pressing down. This gives you a better connection with the ground. With the core engaged, walk the feet up the tree. Keeping one foot connected to the trunk, extend the other leg up. Practice for a couple of breaths, and then switch the legs. Challenge yourself to get lighter with the foot connected to the tree. Exit in reverse order as slowly as possible.

poses.title: Forward Fold
paragraphs: There are 2 primary ways to practice this pose. Beginning with the first way, start in a standing position facing the tree — slightly farther than an arm’s length away from the trunk. Keeping the spine long, hinge at the hips and reach for the tree. Plant the hands directly on the trunk, and then melt the heart down towards the ground. Keep the legs straight, but not locked out — maintaining soft knees. Additionally, you can relax the head through the shoulders. This provides an excellent stretch for both the hamstrings and the muscles of the back.

For the second way, begin facing away from the tree. You want to be as close to the trunk as possible. The legs do not need to touch the tree, however you do want to be very close. Keeping the spine long and hinging at the hips, slowly lower the upper body down towards the ground. To enhance the stretch, reach for the trunk and gently pull the upper body closer to the legs.

poses.title: Handstand
paragraphs: Begin in a forward fold position, facing away from the tree. You may have to play around with the starting position — either moving closer to or farther away from the trunk. Plant the hands on the ground about shoulder-width apart. Often times, people place the hands too far apart. This does not help, and actually makes it harder because of the poor alignment. The fingers should be spread out and almost gripping the ground. However, be mindful with the thumbs. After spreading the fingers out, bring the thumbs back closer to the pointer fingers. With the core active and strong, begin to walk the feet up the tree. Keeping one foot on the trunk, extend the other leg up. Practice for a couple of breaths, and then switch the legs. Exit in reverse order, as mindfully as you can. If you do find yourself falling out of the pose, open to the side you are falling to in order to prevent a tough fall. This way, you can easily land on the feet.

poses.title: Headstand
paragraphs: Begin in tabletop position, facing away from the tree. The feet should be right next to the trunk. This typically allows for the best setup. Make a strong foundation with the forearms. The arms should form an equilateral triangle. Lightly touch the top of the head to the ground in the middle of the forearms. To find where exactly to position the head, place your palm over the center of the forehead. Wherever your middle finger touches is where the head should touch the ground. It is very important to not place excessive weight on the head. It should barely be touching the ground. Keeping the core engaged, walk the feet up the trunk. Keep one foot on the trunk as you extend the other leg up. Practice for a couple of breaths, and then place the other foot on the trunk with the other leg up. For more of a challenge and to prime the body for headstands without support, practice getting lighter with the foot connected to the tree. Exit in reverse order slowly.

poses.title: Heart Opener with Gymnastics Rings
paragraphs: With the gymnastics rings wrapped around the tree, grab ahold of a ring in each hand and begin walking away from the trunk. You should be facing away from the tree, with the arms extended out to the sides. Move very mindfully into this posture, because it can be an extremely deep stretch. When you cannot walk forward any more, pause and root down through the feet. Gently press the heart and the hips forward and take deep belly breaths.

poses.title: Hero Pose
paragraphs: Begin in a kneeling position, facing the tree. You want the knees as close to the trunk as possible. Be extremely mindful with the knees and ankles, especially if you have any issues with these parts of the body. Do not practice this pose if you have any serious issues. Sit back on top of the feet, and find a long spine. Raise the arms in front of the body and place the hands directly on the tree. Keep the shoulders relaxed down away from the ears, and keep the face relaxed as well. Take several deep breaths, maintaining length through the crown of the head.

poses.title: High Boat Pose
paragraphs: Start in a seated position, facing towards the tree. You may have to play around with the distance between you and the tree, but it should be slightly shorter than a leg’s length away. The closer you get to the trunk, the more challenging the pose becomes. Walk the feet up the tree until the legs are fully extended. Keeping the feet planted and the spine long, lean back with the upper body — decreasing the angle between you and the ground. Extend the arms up over the head, and practice for a couple of breaths.

poses.title: Horizontal Lat Stretch
paragraphs: Begin about a foot away from the tree. With either arm, reach for the outside of the trunk and grab it with your hand. Maintaining a strong grip and an elongated spine, start to shift the weight back as you bend the knees and drop the hips. Relax the other arm down by the side or place the hand directly on the hip. Breathe slowly as you gently move deeper into the stretch on exhalations. Practice on both sides.

poses.title: Horse Pose
paragraphs: There are 2 primary ways to practice this pose. The first way is to begin facing the tree, about 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk. With the hands on the trunk, take a wide stance with the toes angled out 45 to 90 degrees. The farther you angle the toes out, the more external rotation you will get with the hips, and the more challenging the pose becomes. The feet should be a good deal apart — 2 or 3 times wider than hip-width. On an inhalation, slowly lower down — keeping the spine long. On an exhalation, drive down through the heels and return to a standing position. You can also hold this pose at the bottom for several breaths, which is an excellent way to open the hips, as well as to improve overall flexibility and strength.

The second way to practice this pose is facing away from the tree — with your back against the trunk. This variation is only to be practiced statically — not dynamically. Keeping the back against the trunk of the tree, find a wide stance with the toes angled out. Bend the knees, drop the hips, and settle into the pose for several breaths. This will build tree trunk strength in the legs.

poses.title: Hula Hoop Hip Circles
paragraphs: Remaining in a seated position for extended periods of time is detrimental to the body. Just 30 minutes of continuous sitting deactivates the core and glutes, as well as the metabolism. It also tightens the hip flexors and psoas — resulting in anterior pelvic tilt. This dynamic movement is the remedy for problems caused by sitting too much.

Begin about a foot away from the trunk, facing the tree. Place the hands on the outsides of the trunk. On an exhalation, circle the hips forward. On an inhalation, circle the hips back. Be as fluid as you can with this movement, and don’t feel as though you need to keep the hands glued to the tree. Adjust the hands accordingly — however results in the best stretch. To make this movement more dynamic, arch the spine as you circle forward, and round the spine as you circle back. Practice for a couple cycles of breath in each direction.

poses.title: Inverted Rows (with Gymnastics Rings)
paragraphs: First, set up the gymnastics rings around the tree. Next, grab the rings and walk away from the trunk. The rings should be waist-height or slightly higher, and you should keep tension with them the entire time. Keeping the core engaged, walk the feet slightly forward as you lean the upper body back. Ideally, you want to position the body at a 45-degree angle to the ground. As you lean back and get into position, keep the arms long. Make sure the body stays like a plank throughout this movement. On an exhalation, pull yourself towards the tree using the back muscles and biceps. Keep the elbows close to the body, as opposed to allowing them to flare out. On an inhalation, slowly return back to the starting position. Practice for a couple of breaths dynamically. You can also hold this pose statically for breaths at the top to greatly strengthen the back.

poses.title: Knees-to-Chest Pose
paragraphs: Start in a supine position, facing away from the tree. The head should be about a foot away from the trunk. Reach behind and grab on to the tree. Lift the legs up and bring the knees in towards the chest. Pause here for a couple of breaths. In addition to holding this stretch statically, you can also find some gentle side-to-side movement. Further, you can also practice this stretch with the arms relaxed down by the sides, or with the hands on the shins.

poses.title: Lateral Leg Swings
paragraphs: A lot of people complain about tight hips. The specific areas of the hip that are typically tight include the hip flexors, the iliotibial bands (outsides of the hips), and the groin muscles (insides of the hips). This is an incredible dynamic move that opens up the hips — especially the areas just mentioned.

Begin an arm’s length away from the tree, and then step back an additional 1 or 2 feet. Lean forward towards the trunk and place both hands firmly on the tree. You want to make sure you have as much stability as possible when practicing this move. Continue to lean slightly forward as you root down through one foot. With the other leg, inhale as you bring it across the midline of the body. On an exhalation, swing the leg up and to the side. Try to kick the leg up as high as possible, but be mindful to properly warm up first. Always move with the breath, even if it is a faster movement pattern. Practice on both sides.

poses.title: Leg Swings
paragraphs: We want to practice consciously slowing down as often as possible, but there is a time and a place for more dynamic and faster movement patterns. This is one of those times, and this movement really opens up the hips, as well as improves overall mobility of the legs. It also increases flexibility in the hamstrings.

Begin on the side of the tree, about an arm’s length away from the trunk. Place the hand of the arm closest to the tree directly on the trunk. Root down through the foot farthest away from the tree. On an inhalation, swing the inside leg back. On an exhalation, swing the leg forward — in front of the body. Even though this is a faster movement, still flow with the breath. Allow yourself to fully warm up the hips, but eventually try to kick the leg up as high as possible. This gets easier to do the more you practice. Additionally, make sure to keep the spine long and the posture strong. Practice on both sides.

poses.title: Legs up the Tree Pose
paragraphs: To enter this pose, begin in a seated position facing the tree. Bring the hips as close to the trunk as possible while you sweep the legs to either side. Lean back and relax the back down on the ground as you extend the legs up — resting them on the tree. Adjust yourself as needed, and move closer to the trunk if you have to. Place the hands on the belly, or rest the arms by the sides. Consciously relax as much as you can. Practice for several minutes — breathing as deeply as possible. Then, mindfully exit in reverse order.

poses.title: Low Boat Pose
paragraphs: Begin in a supine position, with the head about a foot away from the trunk. The legs should be fully extended, relaxed down on the ground. Reach back and grab on to the tree. Next, keeping the legs extended, lift them a few inches off the ground. Pause here and hold this position for several breaths. Maintain length through the toes, and maintain a neutral spine — as opposed to overarching in the lower back. For a greater challenge, gently press the lower back down into the ground.

poses.title: Lunge
paragraphs: Begin facing the tree, with your hands on the trunk. The feet should be close to the trunk — only a few inches away. Mindfully step one leg back. The toes and hips should be squared towards the tree as you bend the lead knee. Use the hands to press against the trunk as you lower the hips deeper. This will help you maintain perfect posture throughout the lunge position, and it will get you deeper into the stretch. Often times, the upper body collapses in the lunge, however the tree prevents this from happening. You can practice this movement dynamically or statically. When practicing dynamically, alternate legs. Step back on an inhalation. Then, on an exhalation, drive down through the lead heel to press back into the starting position. You can also use the hands on the trunk to help pull you back. When practicing statically, settle into a deep lunge position for several breaths on each leg. Remember to press the hands against the trunk for better posture and a better stretch.

poses.title: Mountain Pose
paragraphs: Begin in a standing position, facing away from the tree. You want to be as close to the trunk as possible, but without leaning against it for support. Ground down through the soles of the feet, while also consciously lengthening up through the crown of the head. Keep the heart up, and the shoulders rolled down and back. To fully experience this pose as it is meant to, become like the tree. With the eyes closed, visualize roots growing down through the soles of the feet — deeply into the Earth. Additionally, feel yourself growing higher through the crown toward the sky with each breath. Trees teach us ideal posture. They are always rooting deeper and reaching higher. Take several full breaths in this strong position. You can also practice this pose while facing the tree.

poses.title: Neck Circles
paragraphs: Begin about a foot away from the tree, with both hands planted directly on the trunk. Root down through the feet as you simultaneously lengthen up through the crown. Maintaining maximum length, start to make gentle circles with the neck. Gradually increase the range of motion as you continue to make circles. Move slowly, and relax the jaw. It is especially helpful to allow the mouth to open slightly. Practice in both directions — moving as mindfully as possible.

poses.title: Pigeon Pose
paragraphs: Start in tabletop position, facing the tree. The head should only be a few inches away from the trunk. Bring the left knee towards the left wrist, and then sweep the leg across the body to the right. You do not need to bring the left foot all the way up to the right wrist, but it should be headed in that direction. Make sure the hips are squared up towards the trunk, and find a vertical spine. Melt the hips straight down to the ground. To go deeper, fold the upper body down over the left leg and reach for the tree — grabbing on to the trunk. Stay for several breaths, and then practice on the other side. For the other side, just flip the setup. From tabletop position, bring the right knee to the right wrist, and then sweep the leg across the body to the left. Find a vertical position first, with the hips squared up to the tree. Then, if you want to go deeper, fold down over the right leg. It may feel good to do a few breaths in downward-facing dog in between each side.

poses.title: Pistol Chair Pose
paragraphs: If you thought the regular chair pose was tough, just wait until this one. Most people think pistol squats will forever remain an impossibility for them. However, this does not have to be the case. You can utilize the help of the tree to prime the nervous system and build the necessary strength to one day do the full expression of this pose — free of any support.

Like chair pose, begin facing away from the tree with your back against the trunk. The feet should be together as you bend the knees and lower the hips. Keeping the core engaged, begin to shift the weight onto one foot while extending the other leg out in front. Take a couple breaths on one side, then practice on the other. With Tree Yoga, you can do things you never thought you could.

poses.title: Planks
paragraphs: There are so many ways to practice planks. There are a myriad of expressions and variations — all with their own awesome benefits. Whichever of the different types of planks you decide to practice, ideally you want to do it close to a tree. That way, you not only strengthen the body, but you also improve your energetic health by being in the tree’s positive electromagnetic field. Some examples of planks you can practice include the traditional plank, the forearm plank, the side plank, and the alternate-opposite balance plank. Practice planks often, and always maintain a steady breath.

poses.title: Plow Pose
paragraphs: There are 2 main ways to practice this pose. First, we can have the feet connected to the trunk. Second, we can give ourselves more space. A direct connection to the tree is often best, however we get benefit from just being close to the tree — in the positive electromagnetic field.

For the first way, you will probably have to play around with the starting distance between you and the trunk. Begin in a supine position, with the head and shoulders about 3 or 4 feet away from the tree. Adjust accordingly once you experiment — moving closer or farther away. Bring the knees into the chest. Next, lift the hips and stack them over the shoulders. You can use the arms to help you get into alignment. Send the legs back and over the head — placing the soles of the feet on the tree. Breathe deeply, and walk the feet down the trunk as you become more flexible. It is important to not look left or right in this pose. This can injure the neck. Keep everything in one line — especially the head. For the second way, just start slightly farther away from the tree. Use the same setup. The only difference is that the feet will not be connected to the tree. Instead, relax the legs down towards the ground while they are over the head. As you become more flexible, the toes will eventually touch the ground.

poses.title: Plyometric Push-Ups
paragraphs: Start an arm’s length away from the tree, then move back another foot. You need to be especially mindful with this dynamic movement pattern. If you are not fully present and paying attention to what you are doing, you can get injured with this move. Do not bring the head too close to the tree. On an inhalation, allow yourself to lean forward and fall towards the trunk. Catch yourself by placing both hands on the tree. Then, on an exhalation, explosively press yourself away from the trunk — returning to the starting position. Keep the spine long and the elbows close to the body. Additionally, keep the body in a plank position the entire time. Practice for several rounds of breath.

poses.title: Power Tree Super Charging
paragraphs: Whenever I go walking in Nature, I am always looking for power trees. By power trees, I mean trees with huge electromagnetic fields. This is some of the strongest positive energy you can connect with in life. To find a power tree, look for trees with enormous trunks. This is a sure sign that the tree has an enormous electromagnetic field. Further, remember that the trunk of the tree is the center of the electromagnetic field, so it has the highest concentration of positive energy. Once you have found your power tree, you simply stand next to it and place your hands on the trunk. Take deep conscious breaths. The more relaxed you get, the more positive energy you absorb and the more negative energy you release. In addition to looking for trees with very large trunks, you can also look for trees that are close together. By placing a hand on each of the trees, you can directly connect with multiple power trees simultaneously. Further, you can look for clusters or rings of trees. Stand in the middle of them, and breathe deeply.

poses.title: Prone Centering
paragraphs: This is the most grounding pose I have ever practiced in all of Yoga. Begin in a prone position, fully relaxed down on the ground with the entire body. The head should be only a few inches away from the trunk, with the face towards the ground. It is helpful to use a towel or mat. Additionally, you can place a rolled-up towel where the forehead rests to give yourself some extra space to breathe. Reach the arms toward the trunk, and grab on to the tree as if you were giving it a hug. Breathe deeply as you melt the body down into the ground. Expand the breath in all directions — not just into the belly, but into the back body and side bodies as well. You will be amazed at just how grounding and centering this pose can be.

poses.title: Pull-Ups with Gymnastics Rings
paragraphs: You need a certain type of tree for this move. Find a tree that has strong horizontal branches. Do not use a branch that cannot support your weight. This can cause injury, as well as damage to the tree. Wrap the gymnastics rings around the branch so that they hang down, and adjust the height to give yourself enough space. Grab on to the rings, and lift the feet off the ground. On an exhalation, slowly pull yourself up towards the branch. On an inhalation, slowly lower yourself back down to the starting position. Practice for several rounds of breath, going through the full range of motion.

poses.title: Reclined Butterfly Pose
paragraphs: Start in a supine position, with the knees bent and the feet down. The head should be 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk. Bring the soles of the feet together as the knees slowly fall open to the sides. Relax the legs, and relax the entire body. Release the arms out to the sides, or rest them on the belly. You can also extend the arms overhead — grabbing on to the tree. Take several deep breaths, or even stay in this position for several minutes.

poses.title: Reclined Hip Circles
paragraphs: Begin in a supine position, facing away from the tree. The head should be about a foot away from the trunk. Reach behind you and grab on to the tree. Keeping the back relaxed down and the spine neutral, start to make circles with the hips. The movement should be as fluid as possible — as if you were under the water. Practice for a couple of breaths, and then reverse directions. You can also practice this move with the arms by the sides, or with the hands directly on the knees.

poses.title: Reclined Twist
paragraphs: Begin on the ground in a supine position, with the knees bent and the feet down. The head should be 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk. Bring the knees into the chest. Come back to this knees-to-chest position in between each side. Keep the left leg hugged in as you fully extend the right leg out — relaxing it onto the ground. Use the right hand to gently guide the left leg across the body. Next, extend the left arm out to the left. Relax the body as much as possible, and stay here for several breaths. Come back to center for knees-to-chest pose, and then do the same thing on the other side. The right leg is hugged in, while the left leg is extended out. You take the right leg across the body with the left hand, and extend the right arm out to the right.

This is one of the only poses in Yoga where you do not want any muscles engaged at all. In nearly every other pose, some muscle tension is typically involved — even in static stretches. However, in this pose, let it all go. Relax every part of the body, including the face. I like to end most of my classes and flows with this reclined twist.

poses.title: Reclined Wrist Circles
paragraphs: Begin in a supine position, with the knees bent and the feet down. The head should be relatively close to the trunk. With the elbows down, lift the rest of the forearms up. Keeping the hands open and relaxed, begin to make circles with the wrists. Move slowly, and bring maximum awareness to the wrist joints. Practice for several breaths, and in both directions.

poses.title: Reverse Plank
paragraphs: Begin in a seated position, facing away from the tree. You should be about an arm’s length away from the trunk. With the knees bent and the feet down, place the hands behind the hips. Have the fingers facing towards the hips, or you can angle them out if it makes it easier on the shoulders. Activate the back and lift the heart up through the chest. Next, drive the hips up to match. Extend one leg out at a time as you continue to press the hips up. You can either have the heels down and toes up, or you can plant the soles of the feet down on the ground. The gaze can be forward, or you can relax the head back and send the gaze up. Keep the core engaged, and practice for a couple of breaths.

poses.title: Reverse Tabletop Pose
paragraphs: Begin in a seated position, facing away from the tree. You should be about an arm’s length away from the trunk. With the knees bent and the feet down, plant the hands behind the hips. The fingers should be facing the hips, or you can angle them out if you initially lack the shoulder mobility for the full expression of this pose. Activate the muscles of the back, and lift the heart up through the chest. Drive down through the heels of the hands and feet as you press the hips up towards the sky. You can either keep the gaze forward, or you can relax the head back if that feels okay with the neck. Practice for a couple of breaths before mindfully lowering the hips back down.

poses.title: Revolved Triangle Pose
paragraphs: It is important to note that the version with the tree is slightly different than the regular version. When practicing regularly, the spine is horizontal. In Tree Yoga, the spine remains vertical.

Begin with either foot very close to the tree, with the toes pointing directly at the trunk. Step back with the other leg. The back heel should be down, with the toes angled out. Keep the legs straight, but do not lock out the knees. Further, keep the spine as long as possible the entire time. If the left foot is forward, twist to the left and place the right hand on the left side of the trunk. If the right foot is forward, twist to the right and place the left hand on the right side of the trunk. Those were a lot of different directions, but this pose is not as complicated as it initially sounds. Use the tree as leverage to gently push yourself more deeply into the pose for a couple of breaths on each side.

poses.title: Seated Butterfly Pose
paragraphs: You can practice this pose 2 main ways. For the first way, begin in a seated position facing away from the tree. You should be right at the base of the tree, with the back against the trunk. Bring the soles of the feet together as the knees fall away from each other. Consciously relax as much as possible — allowing the knees to melt down closer towards the ground. Breathe deeply, and relax a little bit more with each exhalation. For the second way, begin in a seated position facing the tree. Bring the soles of the feet together, and allow the knees to fall open. The toes should be close to the trunk. Keeping the spine elongated, reach for the tree and grab on. Use the tree to gently pull yourself deeper into this stretch for a couple of breaths.

poses.title: Seated Forward Fold
paragraphs: Begin in a seated position, facing the tree. Extend the legs fully and place the soles of the feet against the trunk. The legs should be straight, but the knees should not be locked out. Keep the knees soft. Additionally, keep the spine long for the entire stretch. Reach out in front towards the tree. If you have the flexibility, grab on to the tree and use it to gently pull yourself deeper into the stretch. If you cannot reach the tree, you have a few options. First, keep the arms lifted and continue reaching towards the trunk — even if you do not end up making contact with the tree. This will still result in a great stretch. Second, and depending on the width of the trunk you are working with, separate the legs slightly and position the trunk in between the feet, or even the calves. This way, you should be able to reach the tree and use it to help pull you into a better stretch. Practice for several breaths.

poses.title: Side Lunge
paragraphs: This is another lunge variation that is very beneficial to practice. With this particular variation, you are still increasing lower body strength, but also get the added benefit of stretching the inner thigh. Begin facing the tree, with both hands on the trunk. You should be 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk, with a wide stance. The toes should be slightly angled out. On an inhalation, bend one knee to drop the hips down while keeping the other leg straight. With the extended leg, you can keep the sole of the foot down, or you can lift the toes up. Whichever way, on an exhalation, drive down through the heel of the bent knee and press back up to standing. Alternate sides as you move with the breath, or you can hold this position at the bottom for several breaths on each side.

poses.title: Spinal Flossing
paragraphs: Begin in a supine position, facing away from the tree. The head should be about a foot away from the trunk. With the knees bent and the feet down, reach back behind and grab on to the trunk. Next, find a side-to- side motion with the knees — moving with the breath. Exhale as you send the knees to alternate sides, and inhale as you return to center. Continue with this for several rounds of breath. You can also practice this movement with the arms by the sides.

poses.title: Squat
paragraphs: Begin in a standing position, facing the tree — 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk. Place the hands directly on the tree. On an inhalation, slowly walk the hands down the trunk as you lower the hips. On an exhalation, walk the hands up as you drive down through the heels — pressing back up to standing. Actively pressing down through the heels allows you to fully activate the glutes. You can practice these squats dynamically, or find a static hold at the bottom — taking several deep breaths. Additionally, you can add gentle and subtle movements at the bottom of the squat to greatly improve mobility.

With all squats, make sure to keep the spine elongated. The tree really helps with this. Often times, people have trouble maintaining good posture as they lower into a squat. They also have a difficult time getting deeply into the squat position. By utilizing the tree, you can keep perfect posture throughout the squat, as well as get much lower. This greatly improves mobility and strength. It primes the nervous system, and it is the best way to relearn how to squat correctly.

poses.title: Standing Backbend
paragraphs: It is important to note that backbends done with the tree have the potential to be far deeper than any backbend you have ever previously done. Practice with mindfulness, and never be reckless with deep backbending. However, also realize that your body is supposed to be able to move this way. You can regain this natural spinal mobility and openness with practice. You can be free in your body again with Tree Yoga.

Begin facing away from the tree. Depending on how deeply you want to go, position yourself at a different distance from the trunk. For gentler backbends, position yourself more closely to the tree. For deeper backbends, position yourself farther away — up to 3 or 4 feet. On an inhalation, sweep the arms up and over the head. Get as much length as possible here, as you simultaneously remain grounded through the feet. On an exhalation, begin to lift the heart up and press the hips forward as you reach back towards the trunk. Once the hands land on the tree, you can walk them down the trunk for a deeper backbend. For more flexible people, you can even walk the hands all the way down to the ground into wheel pose. To exit the pose, keep the core engaged as you walk the hands back up the trunk. Eventually, release from the tree and return to standing.

poses.title: Standing Balancing Twist
paragraphs: Here, we have another challenging balance pose that is made much more easily accessible with the help of a tree. Balance is essential in life, and Tree Yoga can help you develop that balance. Additionally, Tree Yoga enhances every twist. You get so much deeper into it by using the trunk as leverage.

Begin facing the tree. You should be far enough away so that when you extend one leg forward, the sole of the foot gets planted on the trunk. Before you extend that leg, root down through the other foot. Then with the legs perpendicular to each other, and with the foot of the lifted leg firmly planted on the trunk, begin to twist towards that lifted leg. Place one hand on the outside of the lifted leg, and reach back behind you with the other arm. Make sure that you keep the spine elongated throughout the entire pose. Practice for a couple of breaths on each side. Enter and exit mindfully.

poses.title: Standing Cat/Cow
paragraphs: Your spine is only as healthy as it is flexible. This dynamic movement brings the spine fully through extension and flexion. It both energizes and opens the spine — creating space for more comfort, as well as a stronger mind-body connection. It also provides a tremendous opening of the front body and back body — especially in the abdominals, chest, and upper back.

Begin 1 or 2 feet away from the tree, with the feet hip- width apart. The hands should be placed directly on the trunk. On an inhalation, press the hips forward towards the tree and tilt the heart up to the sky. This results in a nice extension of the spine. On an exhalation, change the hand positioning so that the hands are on the outsides of the trunk. Round the spine, and send the hips back. Use the tree as leverage to help enhance the stretch in the back body and get greater flexion of the spine. Always start slowly, but you can become more dynamic as you continue to breathe with this movement — making the movement bigger with each breath. Practice for a couple cycles of breath.

poses.title: Standing Elbow Circles
paragraphs: Start an arm’s length away from the trunk, with the side body facing the tree. Root down through both feet, and lengthen up through the crown of the head. Maintain strong posture as you plant the inside hand directly on the trunk. Extend the outside arm out to the side. With the motion centered at the elbow joint, begin to make slow and smooth circles with the outside arm. Breathe deeply, and be as mindful as possible with this movement. Practice in both directions, and on both sides. You can also practice with the outside arm relaxed down.

poses.title: Standing Pigeon Pose
paragraphs: Begin in a standing position, facing the tree. You should be close enough to the tree so that you can firmly grab on to the trunk with both hands. Cross the left leg over the right leg so that the left ankle is just above the right knee. Additionally, you want to keep the foot flexed — toes going towards the left knee. Keeping the heart up and the spine long, slowly lower the hips down by bending the right knee. You should immediately start to feel a nice stretch in the left hip. Practice for a couple of breaths, and then exit in reverse order. Repeat on the other side — crossing the right leg over the left leg.

poses.title: Standing Shoulder Circles
paragraphs: Many people have tight shoulders, with the chest collapsing in on itself. The front body is tight, and the back body is weak. Thus, to fix this situation, we need to open the front body, and activate the back body. This movement does just that. Further, it gets you ready for any strength-based upper body moves.

Begin on the side of the tree, about an arm’s length away. Firmly root down through both feet as you simultaneously lengthen up through the crown. Place the hand of the inside arm directly on the trunk, and keep it plugged in for this entire move. On an inhalation, lift the outside arm up in front of the body. On an exhalation, reach and circle that arm back behind the body. Move slowly, and make these circles as big as possible. Further, keep the hand open and relaxed — spreading the fingers wide to create maximum space throughout. Practice in both directions, and on both sides.

poses.title: Standing Side Bend
paragraphs: It is essential to move the spine in all major directions on a daily basis. This includes moving through extension and flexion, but also moving laterally and rotationally. Do not forget about lateral movement, and do not forget about the side body.

Begin about an arm’s length away from the tree, with the side body facing the trunk. The hand of the inside arm should be planted on the tree. On an inhalation, raise the other arm over your head — getting as much length as possible through the fingertips. On an exhalation, side bend towards the trunk of the tree. If you have the flexibility, you can even bring both hands to the trunk. However, do not force this. Length is most important here. Side bend as if you were going up and over a giant barrel — not through it. Practice for a couple of breaths on each side.

poses.title: Single-Leg Ankle Circles
paragraphs: The ankles are the foundation of mobility. If you want good overall mobility, you need to have mobility with the ankles. Further, a problem with the foundation gets worse with time, and it goes up the chain of the body. Lack of ankle mobility will result in poor mobility throughout the body — even the upper body eventually if this issue is not addressed.

Begin on the side of the tree, about 1 or 2 feet away. Grab on to the trunk with the inside arm. Alternatively, start slightly farther away and plant the hand on the trunk. Root down through the inside foot, and lift the other leg in front of the body. Keep the spine long and maintain a steady breath as you make slow circles with the ankle of the lifted leg. Bring as much awareness as possible down to the ankle joint, and make the circles as big as you can. Try to trace a slightly bigger circle each time. Practice in both directions, and on both sides.

poses.title: Single-Leg Hip Circles
paragraphs: Nowadays, it seems like almost everyone has tight hips and lower back pain. This is largely due to lack of movement and lack of flow to the middle of the body. You want to move the hip joint multiple times per day, and one of the best ways to move it is in a circular motion. This move really loosens up the middle of the body, and it is one of the best ways to open the hips.

Begin with the side body facing the tree, 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk. Grab on to the tree — wrapping your arm around the trunk. Alternatively, plant the hand directly on the tree and start slightly farther away. Root down through the foot closest to the tree. Keeping the body upright and the spine long, start to make circles with the outside leg, with the motion centered at the hip joint. Breathe deeply as you move, and go in both directions. Practice on both sides.

poses.title: Standing Single-Leg Knee Circles
paragraphs: If you treat the body like glass, it will respond like glass. So many people do just that with the knee joint. This is not an invitation to be reckless with any movement, but it is an invitation to move in ways you are not used to. I know the knee is a hinge joint, but that does not mean we can’t move it in other ways. I highly encourage you to move all joints in all directions — not just in the ones you are comfortable with, or used to doing. Promote flow throughout the entire body, and you won’t break like glass. Instead, you will be able to bend like a tree.

Start with the side body facing the tree. You want to be about 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk. Wrap the arm closest to the tree around the trunk, or plant the hand directly. Additionally, root down through the foot closest to the tree. Keeping strong posture, lift the outside leg up in front of the body. Next, begin to make circles centered at the knee joint of the lifted leg. Move with the breath, and go in both directions. If you do not like the circular motion with the knee, you can just bend and extend the leg instead. This still promotes flow to that area. Practice this move on both sides.

poses.title: Standing Splits
paragraphs: Start in a standing position, facing the tree. The distance away from the tree will depend on your flexibility, but it is a good idea to start about an arm’s length away. The more flexible you are, the closer you should move to the trunk. Swing either leg up and place the heel or the sole of the foot on the tree. Be mindful not to slam the foot into the trunk. Be as soft as possible with the landing. Keep the spine elongated as you take deep breaths — stretching the back of the lifted leg. If you are close enough to the trunk, you can grab on to it with the hands and pull yourself closer for a deeper stretch. Practice on both sides.

poses.title: Standing Wrist Circles
paragraphs: Begin an arm’s length away from the trunk, with the side body facing the tree. Plant the inside hand directly on the trunk. Extend the outside arm to the side. Maintain good posture as you make wrist circles with the outside arm. The hand should be open and relaxed. Even though it is a small circle, don’t go fast. Take your time and bring as much awareness as possible to the wrist joint. Breathe deeply as you practice in both directions, and on both sides. You can also practice this move with the outside arm relaxed down.

poses.title: Supine Centering
paragraphs: In a world of speed and stimulation, it is highly beneficial to get low to the ground. When you bring the body close to the ground, negative energy is released. This works through the nervous system. It works best if you can bring areas of highly concentrated nerves close to the Earth. Nerves are not just concentrated in the brain, but also in the heart, stomach, and trunk — as well as in the hands and feet. The closer you bring these areas to the ground, the better the energetic connection is established between you and the Earth — allowing negative energy to flow out, and positive energy to flow in.

Facing either towards or away from the tree, lower yourself onto the back. Extend the arms and the legs out, or into a position of choice. One option is to have the knees bent and the feet down. Consciously relax the body as much as you can. Let all the negative energy flow right out of you into the ground. Stay here for several minutes, breathing deeply.

poses.title: Tabletop Alternate Balance Pose
paragraphs: Begin in tabletop position, facing the tree. The head should be about 2 feet away from the trunk, but you may need to move closer in or farther away — depending upon the length of your arms. Extend either arm forward, planting the hand directly on the trunk. Extend the opposite-side leg back. Make sure to actively press back through the heel to fully activate the core. Additionally, maintain a neutral cervical spine — aligned with the rest of the spine. Practice for a couple of breaths, and then switch sides — doing this pose with the other arm and the other leg.

poses.title: Tabletop Same-Side Balance Pose
paragraphs: Start in tabletop position, facing the tree. The head should be about 2 feet away, but you may need to adjust depending on the length of your arms. Keep the body as square as possible to the ground for the entire time, as opposed to tilting up and to the side. Fully extend either arm forward, and plant the hand directly on the tree. Then, extend the same-side leg back — pressing through the heel. Practice for a couple of breaths, and then do the same thing on the other side.

poses.title: Tabletop Side Body Stretch
paragraphs: Begin in tabletop position, facing towards the tree. Your head should be only a few inches away from the trunk. Take the left leg diagonally across behind you to the right — touching down with the toes, or with the inside of the foot. Then, take the left arm and reach for the trunk. Grab on to the tree, and use it as leverage for a deep side body stretch. Gently tilt the heart up. This will greatly enhance the stretch and the opening of the lateral chain. Make sure that the right hand is directly rooted under the shoulder, and maintain a steady breath. Practice on both sides — taking the right leg diagonally across to the left next, and bringing the right hand to the trunk.

poses.title: Tree Hug Pose
paragraphs: The closer you bring the body to the tree, the more negative energy you release, and the more positive energy you absorb. There are not just high concentrations of nerves in the hands and feet, but also in the stomach, heart, and face. Don’t forget about the brain itself. By bringing all these parts of the body close to the tree, you establish the strongest connection possible — allowing for the best energy flow. Connection is one of the main things people crave, as well as one of the most important things people are missing. This pose can quite literally reconnect you to the feeling of connection. Remember, the tree is alive. It does not have arms, but it is energetically hugging you back.

Get as close as possible to the tree and wrap your arms around the trunk — giving the tree a hug. Hug the tree as if you were hugging someone you love. The face can be right against the trunk, or turned to the side. Breathe deeply in this position for several minutes.

poses.title: Tree Plugging Pose
paragraphs: Start in a standing position, facing the tree. You should be 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk. Place both hands on the tree to establish a direct connection. Remember, the hands have high concentrations of nerves which allows for great energy flow. Root down through the feet as you lengthen up through the crown. Roll the shoulders back and down away from the ears — opening the front of the body. Breathe deeply in this position. Placing the hands on the tree is one of the absolute best ways to release negative energy and stress. It also connects us with some of the purest positive energy there is.

poses.title: Tree Pose
paragraphs: It wouldn’t be Tree Yoga if there wasn’t a Tree Pose. There are 2 primary setups for this pose. For the first, begin close to the tree — only a few inches away from the trunk. With the side body next to the tree, wrap the same-side arm around the trunk as you root down through the foot closest to the tree. Externally rotate the outside hip, and place the sole of the foot on the inside of the planted calf or thigh. Alternatively, you can keep the toes lightly touching the ground as you bring the heel to the ankle. Do not place the lifted foot on the knee. This puts the knee in a vulnerable position. The outside arm can be relaxed down, or extended up. The second setup for this pose is exactly the same as the first, only you are not wrapping the arm around the trunk. Instead, the hand is planted on the tree. Thus, you want to start slightly farther away from the trunk. Practice for several breaths on each side.

poses.title: Tree Root Super Charging
paragraphs: I will never forget when I first discovered the power of connecting with the roots of a tree. I was in the White Mountains of New Hampshire with my Brother. We had just walked through the Flume Gorge when I noticed a fascinating tree. The tree had grown on top of a boulder, and the roots wrapped around the giant rock. Thus, they were exposed and you could grab on to them. I grabbed on to the roots of this tree and started doing some deep breaths. The next thing that happened is simply incredible. A chipmunk ran up to me and began watching me do Tree Yoga. After a few moments of watching, the chipmunk walked over and sat down on top of my left foot. I was blown away. Chipmunks are typically so skittish, and they rarely come close to people. Yet, I had one sitting on my foot just minutes after this discovery.

The roots of a tree are the most grounding part of a tree. This energy is needed nowadays more than ever. The majority of people live completely cerebral lives, with all of their energy always centered in the brain. Additionally, they are often going a hundred different directions at a hundred miles per hour. We all can benefit from slowing down and practicing more grounding, and there is nothing more grounding than the roots of a tree. Once you find a tree you can work with, just grab on to the roots and breathe deeply. That is all you have to do, and you will feel more centered than ever.

poses.title: Triangle Pose
paragraphs: You will be absolutely blown away at how much better triangle pose is with the tree. Not only is it much easier to practice, but the stretch is greatly enhanced. However, be mindful with this pose. This is a pose you want to be warmed up for, and it is a pose you want to be especially careful with in the colder weather. Utilize the tree, but always do it mindfully.

Begin with one foot close to the tree, with the toes pointed directly to the trunk. Step back 3 or 4 feet with the other leg. The back heel should be down, with the toes angled out. Keep the legs straight, but do not lock out the knees. Additionally, keep the core engaged and the spine elongated. Hinge at the lead hip, and place both hands on the trunk. One hand should be high, and the other one should be low — close to the ground. Use the tree as leverage to move yourself more deeply into this side body stretch by tilting the heart up towards the sky. Practice for a couple of breaths on each side.

poses.title: Twisting Lunge
paragraphs: Remember, lunges are an essential movement pattern. Lunges are something you want to practice daily. They strengthen the legs in a balanced way, and they also fix tight hip flexors. There are many different variations of lunges. This particular variation adds a twist to the mix. This twisting improves spinal mobility, and it also enhances the stretch in the hip flexor.

Begin facing the tree, with the feet close to the trunk — a few inches away. Step back with one leg and settle into the regular lunge position. Next, use the same-side arm to plant the hand on the outside of the tree. This is the part that has the potential to be confusing. For clarity, if you step back with the left leg, use the left arm on the tree. Specifically, place the left hand on the right side of the trunk. Then, use this hand as leverage to take you deeper into the twist. Practice for a couple of breaths on each side.

poses.title: Upward-Facing Dog
paragraphs: Begin in tabletop position, facing the tree. Slowly lower yourself into a prone position, with the belly down on the ground. The head should be very close to the trunk. Start to look towards the tree as you walk the hands up the trunk. Actively press the hands into the tree and lift the heart up. Roll the shoulders down and back away from the ears. You should feel a deep stretch all throughout the front of the body. Practice for several breaths, then exit in reverse order.

poses.title: Vertical Lat Stretch
paragraphs: Begin facing the tree — about an arm’s length away. Extend one arm up and plant the hand on the trunk. Keeping the hand planted, hinge at the hip, and allow the upper body to begin to relax down towards the ground. Take several deep breaths. Maintain a long spine throughout this stretch, and practice on both sides. Enter and exit as mindfully as possible.

poses.title: Warrior I
paragraphs: Begin with one foot close to the tree, with the toes directly towards the trunk. Step back with the other leg about 4 or 5 feet. The heel should be down, with the toes angled out. Additionally, the hips should be squared towards the tree. With both hands on the trunk, bend the lead knee and drop the hips down — keeping the back leg straight. A common problem in this pose occurs when the weight is shifted too far forward. Ideally, we want the weight slightly shifted back. The tree can help with that. The more you press into the trunk with the hands, the more the weight will shift back. Further, the harder you press, the deeper you get into the pose. Take a couple of breaths on each side.

poses.title: Warrior II
paragraphs: Begin with one foot close to the tree, with the toes facing the trunk. Step back 4 or 5 feet with the other leg. The back heel should be melted down, with the toes angled out. We don’t want the hips and belly button squared towards the trunk. We want them squared towards the side — perpendicular to the lead toes. Place the lead hand directly on the trunk, and extend the other arm back. Bend the lead knee and keep the back leg straight as you lower down. Utilize the tree. Press the hand on the trunk into the tree to help shift the weight back and drop more deeply into the pose. Practice for a couple of breaths on each side.

poses.title: Warrior III
paragraphs: Begin an arm’s length away from the tree, then step back an additional 1 or 2 feet. The extra distance is essential for optimal alignment in this pose. Keep the toes and the hips squared towards the tree. Further, keep the spine long and the core engaged. Root down through one foot, and hinge at the hips as you extend the other leg back. The arms and the extended back leg should be parallel to the ground — both perpendicular to the planted leg. Keep the neck and cervical spine aligned with the rest of the spine, as opposed to tilting the head up. Press the hands into the trunk, and also press back through the heel of the lifted leg. Practice for a couple of breaths on each side. To prime the nervous system for better balance, and for a greater challenge, you can get lighter with the hands over time. Even more challenging, you can close the eyes.

poses.title: Wheel Pose
paragraphs: Begin in a supine position. You should be 1 or 2 feet away from the trunk. Keeping the legs about hip-width apart, bend the knees and place the feet down. A lot of people have the legs too wide in this pose. Make sure you do not go wider than hip-width with the legs. The same goes for the arms. Don’t go much wider than shoulder-width. Bend the elbows and plant the hands down by the shoulders — just outside the head. Keep the core engaged and fire the glutes as you press down through the hands and feet. Drive the hips up as high as possible. Adjust the hands and feet as needed. Practice for several breaths, and then lower down as mindfully as you can. Tuck the chin, and touch down with the shoulders first, then lower the hips all the way to the ground.

poses.title: Wide V-Sit
paragraphs: Start in a seated position, facing the tree. Send the legs out into a wide “V shape”. Keeping the spine long throughout the pose, reach out in front and grab on to the tree. Use the tree to help pull you deeper into the stretch. Practice for several deep breaths. You may have to play around with the distance between you and the tree. Initially, start closer to the tree. However, once your flexibility improves, set up farther away from the trunk.

poses.title: Yoga Nidra
paragraphs: This is the Yoga of conscious sleep. The quality of our sleep is so essential. We want to have the highest quality sleep possible, and this can realized by utilizing the electromagnetic field of the tree. Begin in a reclined position, relatively close to the tree. Let go of everything you do not need in this moment. Bring all of your awareness to the breath. Take low and slow deep breaths from the belly. Close the eyes, and go within. Practice for several minutes, or even 30 minutes and beyond.

You can take this to higher levels. Taking naps next to a tree is the ideal place to take a nap, once again, because you are in the electromagnetic field of the tree. You can also sleep next to trees. I have a 10-foot tree in my bedroom that I sleep next to. The trunk of the tree is located right next to my head. This way, I sleep in positive energy. Camping is another way you can do this.
